value: traveling-wave velocity along the hearing organ rises from 4 to 12 m/s as stimulus frequency rises from 6 to 48 kHz
method: laser Doppler vibrometry of the hearing organ (laser focussed on the scolopidia through a small window opened above the organ), tone stimuli 6 to 60 kHz; only points with coherence above 90% counted as valid; sound pressure calibrated with a Bruel & Kjaer 2610 calibrator
conditions: Animals bred in the authors' in-house facility in Frankfurt am Main (laboratory colony, not wild-caught). Figure 3 caption: data points from nine different animals fitted with an exponential function; one Results sample size is given elsewhere (total phase accumulation 256 +/- 6.2 degrees, n = 6). Sex, sound level and variability of the velocity values are not stated in the Methods the page tool returned; no non-responding preparations are mentioned. The abstract states the tonotopic location of the travelling-wave peak was exponentially related to stimulus frequency. The velocity and frequency range are from this one sentence; no test statistics are attached.

units: ms (preferred echo-response latency to electrical playbacks)
method: playback of electric organ discharge sequences from a mobile dummy fish to freely behaving fish; EOD timing recorded and latency of the fish's discharge after each playback pulse analysed
conditions: Eight Mormyrus rume proboscirostris (standard length 98 to 170 mm; 5 identified as male, 3 presumed female), bred in captivity at Humboldt University of Berlin and kept in pairs, physically separated by a water-permeable barrier, in tropical-condition tanks. Seven playback sequences, each given ten successful presentations per fish in randomized order, inter-trial interval at least 10 min. Results: all animals showed a preferred-latency (echo) response and a latency-avoidance response (about 15 ms) in response to every playback. The paper also reports no consistent difference in the observed-to-expected echo latency ratio across playback inter-discharge-interval patterns, a trend only for post-subtraction cross-correlation differences across playbacks (chi2(6) = 11.571, p = 0.072), and no significant playback effect on lateral probing, va-et-vient or touch (p = 0.131 to 0.397); those results are not logged here. Dummy EOD playback amplitude was 19.05 Vp-p against 13.87 Vp-p for the largest test fish (tool summary).

method: anatomical: peak density of retinal neural cells in retinal wholemounts (counts at 0.25 mm intervals with a 50 x 50 um counting frame, about 400 sample locations; ganglion and amacrine cells could not be told apart in the high-density areas, so all neural cells were counted together and retinal ganglion cells were assumed to be the limit on resolving power); acuity calculated from peak density and focal length as outlined by Lisney & Collin (2008)
conditions: Three left retinas from three euthanised wild-caught fish bought from a local aquarium supplier in Sydney, Australia (the paper's behavioural and video work used other fish; standard length of the three retina fish not given in the text read). The value is a calculated anatomical upper bound, with all neural cells counted together; the paper separately estimates behavioural acuity at about 1.1 cycles/degree from an assumed ratio of about half the anatomical value, not a measurement. Peak density is the mean across the three fish (28,983 cells/mm2); no per-fish values or variance were read.
